topics.title: Graphs
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: Plot and draw lines through given points. (u, s)
Choose and use appropriate scales. (u, s)
Draw, read and interpret the graph (e.g. Distance-Time and Speed-Time Graphs to estimate distance, speed and time). (u, s, v/a)

body.text: To draw a graph from a relation, first tabulate values: choose several x values, work out the matching y values from the relation, then plot the points and join them. Pick a scale for each axis that fits the data on the grid and is easy to read (e.g. 1 square = 10 units, not 1 square = 7 units).

A distance-time graph plots distance travelled (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis). The steepness (gradient) of the line at any point is the speed at that moment: a steeper line means faster travel, a flat (horizontal) section means the object has stopped.

A cyclist travels 20 km in the first hour, rests for 30 minutes, then travels a further 15 km in 45 minutes. Reading the distance-time graph: speed for the first hour = 20 km ÷ 1 h = 20 km/h; during the rest, distance stays flat at 20 km; speed for the last section = 15 km ÷ 0.75 h = 20 km/h.

body.expr: speed = distance ÷ time:  20 km ÷ 1 h = 20 km/h,   15 km ÷ 0.75 h = 20 km/h

body.text: A speed-time graph plots speed against time instead. Here the gradient represents acceleration, and the area under the graph between two times gives the distance travelled in that interval.
